subject: Art & Design
title: French New Wave: Breaking Every Rule
description: A micro-lesson that makes French New Wave: Breaking Every Rule usable.

hook.text: Jean-Luc Godard's jump cuts in Breathless shocked critics. He'd cut mid-sentence, mid-action. On purpose.

buildup.text: The French New Wave (late 1950s) was led by young critics who became directors: Godard, Truffaut, Varda.

discovery.text: They shot on streets with handheld cameras, improvised dialogue, and broke the fourth wall.

twist.text: They wrote about cinema before making it. Their criticism shaped their filmmaking philosophy.

climax.text: New Wave's influence is everywhere: Tarantino, Wes Anderson, and modern indie cinema all carry its DNA.

punchline.text: They proved that the rules of cinema exist so someone can break them.

quiz.question: What was a signature technique of French New Wave filmmakers?
options: Jump cuts, handheld cameras, and breaking the fourth wall
Perfect continuity editing and studio lighting
Only shooting in black and white

details.summary: The French New Wave of the late 1950s–60s shattered Hollywood conventions with jump cuts, handheld cameras, location shooting, and improvised dialogue. Directors like Godard and Truffaut made personal, low-budget films that proved cinema could be revolutionary, intellectual.
details.whyItMatters: The New Wave proved anyone with a camera and ideas could make cinema. Its rebellion against studio filmmaking empowered independent cinema worldwide and invented techniques that remain standard in modern filmmaking.
takeaways: Jump cuts and handheld cameras shattered Hollywood conventions
Godard and Truffaut pioneered personal, low-budget filmmaking
The movement empowered independent cinema worldwide

faq.question: What rules did the French New Wave break?
faq.answer: Classical Hollywood demanded invisible editing, studio lighting, scripted dialogue, and linear narratives. New Wave films used jump cuts, natural light, improvised scenes, direct-to-camera addresses, and non-linear storytelling.

faq.question: Why were critics-turned-directors so revolutionary?
faq.answer: Truffaut, Godard, Rohmer, and Chabrol wrote for Cahiers du Cinéma before making films. Their deep knowledge of cinema history let them consciously deconstruct conventions. They knew exactly which rules they were breaking and why, making their rebellion intellectually purposeful.
